Likelihood ratio test for nested uncounted models

Source: R/model_comparison.R
lrtest.Rd

Performs a likelihood ratio test between two nested uncounted models fitted by maximum likelihood (Poisson or Negative Binomial). The test statistic is

Usage

lrtest(object1, object2, test = c("LR", "Wald"))

Arguments

object1

An "uncounted" model (Poisson or NB).

object2

An "uncounted" model (Poisson or NB). The function automatically identifies the simpler model regardless of argument order.

test

"LR" (default) for the likelihood ratio test, or "Wald" for a robust Wald test (see Details).

Value

An object of class "uncounted_lrtest" with components test, statistic, df, p_value, boundary, dispersion, model descriptions, and log-likelihoods. For test = "Wald" also vcov_type.

Details

$$LR = 2\bigl(\ell_2 - \ell_1\bigr)$$

where \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) are the maximised log-likelihoods of the simpler and more complex models, respectively. Under \(H_0\) the statistic follows a \(\chi^2\) distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the difference in the number of estimated parameters.

Boundary correction for Poisson vs NB. When comparing a Poisson model (H0) against a Negative Binomial model (H1), the dispersion parameter \(\theta\) lies on the boundary of its parameter space under \(H_0\) (\(\theta \to \infty\)). The standard \(\chi^2\) approximation is invalid in this setting. Following Chernoff (1954) and Self & Liang (1987), with \(q\) further parameters tested at interior points (covariates in the NB model only), the p-value is

$$p = 0.5\,\Pr(\chi^2_q > LR) + 0.5\,\Pr(\chi^2_{q+1} > LR)$$

where \(\chi^2_0\) is a point mass at zero. With the same mean model (\(q = 0\)) this is \(0.5\Pr(\chi^2_1 > LR)\) for \(LR > 0\) and 1 for \(LR = 0\), which happens with probability one half under \(H_0\).

Nesting. A Poisson model is nested in an NB model only if its alpha, beta and gamma specifications are contained in the NB model's. An NB model is never nested in a Poisson model, however many covariates the Poisson model has, so such pairs are an error: use compare_models for them. For two models of the same family, specifications that are not nested give a warning.

Overdispersion. The \(\chi^2\) reference also needs the larger model to be correctly specified. Otherwise the statistic converges to \(\sum_j \lambda_j Z_j^2\), where \(\lambda_j\) are eigenvalues of \(A^{-1}B\) in the tested directions, \(A\) is the Hessian and \(B\) the outer product of the scores (Kent, 1982; White, 1982). With overdispersion the \(\lambda_j\) are roughly the dispersion, so comparing two Poisson models rejects far too often: at a nominal 5\ NB size of 2 and an irrelevant covariate. The result therefore includes the Pearson dispersion of the larger model (NA for Poisson against NB, which tests overdispersion itself), and printing adds a note when it exceeds 1.5. The same applies to weights that are not frequency weights, since the weighted log-likelihood is then a pseudo-likelihood.

Robust alternative. test = "Wald" tests the larger model's extra alpha and beta coefficients with its stored covariance (the robust sandwich by default), \((Rb)'(RVR')^{-1}(Rb) \sim \chi^2_r\), and stays near its nominal level under overdispersion (about 8\ with n = 200). It needs two models of the same method, with the same gamma specification and constraint setting, so it does not cover Poisson against NB or comparisons of gamma specifications.

This function is intended for comparing count models only (Poisson and NB). OLS/NLS models are not supported because they use a pseudo-log-likelihood. The models must be fitted to the same observations and weights: the same observed, auxiliary, reference_pop and weights.

References

Chernoff, H. (1954). On the distribution of the likelihood ratio. Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 25(3), 573–578. doi:10.1214/aoms/1177728725

Kent, J. T. (1982). Robust properties of likelihood ratio tests. Biometrika, 69(1), 19–27. doi:10.1093/biomet/69.1.19

Self, S. G. and Liang, K.-Y. (1987). Asymptotic properties of maximum likelihood estimators and likelihood ratio tests under nonstandard conditions. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 82(398), 605–610. doi:10.1080/01621459.1987.10478472

White, H. (1982). Maximum likelihood estimation of misspecified models. Econometrica, 50(1), 1–25. doi:10.2307/1912526

Examples

set.seed(42)
df <- data.frame(
  N = rep(1000, 30),
  n = rpois(30, lambda = 50)
)
df$m <- rpois(30, lambda = df$N^0.5 * (df$n / df$N)^0.8)

fit_po <- estimate_hidden_pop(data = df, observed = ~m, auxiliary = ~n,
                              reference_pop = ~N, method = "poisson")
#> Warning: Some alpha values < 0 (min = -1.28). Consider using constrained = TRUE.
#> Estimated gamma is at its upper bound (0.5); the optimum may lie outside gamma_bounds = c(1e-10, 0.5).
fit_nb <- estimate_hidden_pop(data = df, observed = ~m, auxiliary = ~n,
                              reference_pop = ~N, method = "nb")
#> Warning: Some alpha values < 0 (min = -1.28). Consider using constrained = TRUE.
#> Estimated gamma is at its upper bound (0.5); the optimum may lie outside gamma_bounds = c(1e-10, 0.5).

# Test for overdispersion (Poisson vs NB)
lrtest(fit_po, fit_nb)
#> Likelihood ratio test
#> ---------------------------------------- 
#> Model 1: POISSON   (logLik = -52.51 )
#> Model 2: NB   (logLik = -52.51 )
#> LR statistic: 0 on 1 df
#> (Boundary-corrected: 0.5 * chi2_0 + 0.5 * chi2_1, Self & Liang 1987)
#> p-value: 1
